items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Pentagon is moving forward with plans to invest in manufacturing capacity for the space industrial base, awarding multiple contracts in recent weeks to companies who supply key space components and subsystems as well as firms with innovative manufacturing technology that’s ready to scale. The Defense Innovation Unit, a Pentagon technology hub designed to help funnel promising commercial capabilities to the military at scale, awarded other transaction agreements in July and August to two comp
items.body:
The Pentagon is moving forward with plans to invest in manufacturing capacity for the space industrial base, awarding multiple contracts in recent weeks to companies who supply key space components and subsystems as well as firms with innovative manufacturing technology that’s ready to scale.

The Defense Innovation Unit, a Pentagon technology hub designed to help funnel promising commercial capabilities to the military at scale, awarded other transaction agreements in July and August to two companies through its Adaptive Space Manufacturing and Integration Scale project. The effort aims to leverage commercially available tools and adaptive manufacturing processes to kick-start higher production rates across the space industrial base.

ALL.SPACE, a firm owned by York Space Systems, was one of those recipients. The company said in an Aug. 31 statement that it will demonstrate on-demand production of its Hydra satellite communications terminal with the goal of producing hundreds of units per month and potentially thousands per year.

“This award reflects a fundamental shift in how defense capabilities are being fielded,” ALL.SPACE Chief Operating Officer Rod McCurdy said in a statement. “Hydra was designed to deliver resilient connectivity across multiple networks and orbits, and this effort provides an opportunity to demonstrate how those capabilities can be delivered at the pace required by next-generation space and defense architectures.”

A second company, Freeform Future Corp., received a contract in July to scale its production of key propulsion and structural hardware. Earlier this year, the company unveiled a laser-based additive manufacturing platform called Skyfall, which it says will significantly expand its production.

Separate from the DIU awards, the Pentagon announced Sept. 1 it would invest $11.4 million in Stellant Systems, a company that makes vacuum tubes that can amplify certain radio frequency signals. In a statement, the Pentagon said it would use Defense Production Act funds to support qualification of the company’s space-based amplifier and to boost production rates, which it says “will greatly reduce schedule, cost, and performance risks to U.S. government satellite programs.”

The Space Force is preparing for a sizable increase in the number of satellites it operates. Deputy Chief of Space Operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements Gen. David N. Miller Jr. said in May that the service’s five-year budget projection includes “thousands” of satellites. Those will fall across a number of mission areas, including space-based moving target indication, data transport, missile warning, and space domain awareness.

In May, the Space Force awarded more than $4 billion to SpaceX to build out a new Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator constellation and another $2.3 billion contract to field satellites as part of its Space Data Network program. It’s also planning to launch new fleets of surveillance and reconnaissance satellites starting in 2029. The service hasn’t said how many spacecraft these constellations will include, but officials have said hitting these numbers will require significant expansion of current production capacity .

“If a company is nominally making 10, we want you to be prepared to make 40,” Space Systems Command Commander Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant said in April. “We want industry to make the investments in capitalization and facilitization, and in return you’re going to get these large production contracts.”

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink has said he’s interested in awarding multiyear procurement contracts for both aircraft and satellites. He told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the goal is to give industry the demand signal it needs to make investments in its manufacturing capacity.

“When the future is uncertain, it’s hard for industry to make those investments to either modernize their facilities or do what they need to do to get to the production capacity we need,” Meink said. “So those long-term deals are a huge part of that.”

items.body:
President Donald Trump on Aug. 28 announced plans to establish a U.S. Space Academy to bolster the country’s workforce and educate “the next generation” of space experts.

The announcement quickly drew comparisons to existing military academies—in a speech at NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, Trump himself likened it to the Army’s United States Military Academy at West Point. But the White House executive order issued in conjunction with the president’s announcement indicates the vision is for a new kind of federal service academy, one led by NASA and designed to train space operators and engineers across the civil, military, and commercial sectors.

“To continue to lead the world in space exploration and technology, while securing and defending our national interests in space, the Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the order states. “It is my administration’s policy to strengthen the nation’s space workforce by expanding opportunities to educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”

The President doesn’t have the authority to create the academy on his own—that would require an act of Congress—but his order establishes a commission to explore questions around the academy’s structure, potential military or civil service requirements, location, funding, and eligibility requirements. The group will be led by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and other commissioners will include leaders from the White House and the Pentagon, including the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Air Force. The commission is meant to issue a report with recommendations by late December.

As those recommendations take shape in the coming weeks and months, experts say they’ll be watching for more detail on the academy’s mission and scope as well as efforts to garner feedback from members of Congress. They’ll also be tracking the U.S. military’s role in the organization and how it might impact the U.S. Air Force Academy, whose 2026 class included 93 Guardians . A Department of the Air Force spokesperson declined to comment for this story. In a statement, USAFA’s Association and Foundation, its alumni organization, said it will “closely monitor developments” and share relevant information with graduates.

Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence, said the concept of a NASA-led “space center of excellence” makes sense given NASA’s deep knowledge and legacy operating in the domain.

“For decades, NASA has been the repository of knowledge when it comes to space operations,” Galbreath said. “It stands to reason that it would be useful to codify that, to create an academy where NASA experts could pass on that knowledge to the next generation.”

While the President’s order doesn’t specify the primary audience for the new academy, Galbreath said there’s an opportunity to reach a wide swath of the space community—from undergraduates to mid-career operators—with programming that ranges from certifications to academic degrees. For the military, the academy could eventually serve as a means for commissioning officers, but Galbreath said that may not be necessary immediately given the Space Force’s small size.

“At some point in the future, it could grow and become a commissioning source, I suppose,” he said. “But we’re still a long way from that.”

Todd Harrison, a space policy expert at the American Enterprise Institute, said that while he agrees there’s a need to expand the space workforce, it’s not clear that a new federally run academy is the right answer. In an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, he cited concerns about operational costs, blurring the line between military and civil space missions, and setting up unnecessary competition with the universities that already exist to train the aerospace workforce.

Harrison suggested that rather than create a separate academy, the administration could start a scholarship program similar to the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps, or ROTC. In this scenario, the government would offer scholarships to students pursuing relevant, space-related degrees in exchange for a period of service in the Space Force, NASA, or another federal agency.

“Instead of competing with our world-class institutions . . . you would let them produce the best and the brightest talent with a commitment to go into the government and work for the government for a period of time,” he said. “Establishing a physical academy is going to take years, whereas if you make it a scholarship program, you could literally start awarding scholarships next school year.”

While a scholarship program is one way to address the government’s workforce pipeline, Galbreath argued there’s also value in creating the consolidated hub of space expertise that would come with the academy model.

“When you have people that are colocated, they’re going to breed new ideas as well,” he said. “If you’re a student and you’re learning about orbital mechanics from a NASA PhD who designed the trajectories for a multi-planetary flyby, you’re getting the best.”

Another key question for the commission is where to locate the academy. Galbreath said it’s worth considering whether the academy should be located in a single campus or dispersed across multiple hubs, adding that cost will be an important factor as the commission considers its footprint.

Harrison cautioned that opening that discussion—which is often loaded with parochial politics—too soon could muddy the process. In fact, some lawmakers have already started to pitch their districts to house the Space Academy, including Rep. Dale Strong, R-Ala., who said on Aug. 31 that Huntsville, Ala., has been floated as a potential location. Although the commission has months to recommend a location, Trump indicated he may select one sooner.

Political headwinds may become a problem for Trump’s Space Academy proposal, especially if Republicans lose their majority in either the House or Senate after midterm elections in November. Harrison said there’s likely not enough time for the commission to complete its work and put the decision to a vote before the end of this legislative session.

But Galbreath noted that creating a new academy could garner bipartisan support, similar to the creation of the Space Force in 2019 during Trump’s first term.

“It’s really going to come down to the cost-benefit—can they make a compelling case that this Space Academy is going to be worth the investment of time and money and personnel,” he said. “If they can, then I think they’ll get bipartisan support. I don’t think this is one of those areas that you can get unilateral support.”

Some Democrats, including Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., have already indicated they’re intrigued by the concept. In an Aug. 28 post on the social media site X, Whitesides said the idea “deserves consideration” but raised concerns about funding and the lack of congressional representation on the commission.

“I am open-minded to hear thoughtful answers to these questions, but I recommend that Congress be engaged quickly and substantively or else this intriguing idea will be stuck on the launch pad,” Whitesides said.

The post What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

items.body:
The Air Force has pulled a piece of testing equipment for its Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles after discovering some appeared to be contaminated with a possible carcinogen .

The order to stop using the AN/PRM-10 test oscillator set came after an Airman discovered polychlorinated biphenyl, or PCB, residue on one of the units during a routine inspection in August, Air Force Global Strike Command said in an Aug. 28 statement.

The Airman, who was at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo., reported the residue and received medical attention for the exposure before returning to duty, according to the statement

The EPA has concluded PCBs are a probable cause of cancer in humans , as well as having negative immune system, reproductive, developmental, and neurological effects. PCBs were regularly used in electrical, heat transfer, and hydraulic equipment for about 50 years due to the compound’s electrical insulating properties , high boiling point, and nonflammibility, until they were banned in 1979 as evidence grew that the compound was toxic to people and the environment.

The AN/PRM-10 test oscillator set is a signal generator used to examine ICBM communications systems, per the Global Strike Command statement. After the Airman reported the issue and tests confirmed the presence of PCBs on that test unit, the 20th Air Force—which oversees ICBM bases—ordered all AN/PRM-10 kits be inspected.

That review of all AN/PRM-10 kits was done within three days, and officials found potential PCB residue on six of eight systems. Samples collected from those systems are now being tested. Officials also ordered safety warnings, precautions, and mandatory personal protective equipment requirements be updated where other legacy test units are still used.

But all AN/PRM-10 systems have been pulled from use in the 20th, and units are transitioning to a modern replacement tester that is free of PCBs, Air Force Global Strike Command said. Leaders are working with the Minuteman III systems program office to dispose of any existing AN/PRM-10 kits and identify any other test equipment pieces that may have PCBs.

The “20th Air Force takes the responsibility to protect our Airmen very seriously,” Commander Maj. Gen. Colin Connor said in a statement. “As our Airmen are our greatest asset, their safety and health are my top priority.”

Concerns about rates of cancer among missileers and other Airmen who work with ICBMs has grown in recent years. In 2023, the Air Force launched a study dubbed the Missile Community Cancer Study to review the possibility of clusters of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma at ICBM bases, as well as other specific cancer concerns raised by the community.

The Torchlight Initiative, an organization made up of current and former ICBM community members and their families that pushes the government to address higher rates of cancer and other illnesses among ICBM airmen, called the swift removal of those units “a great start.” But more work remains to be done, the organization said on social media.

“We need to create a culture where Airmen recognize hazards, speak up, and leaders respond—making the mission safer for those serving today and tomorrow,” Torchlight said in a post on LinkedIn.

Torchlight Initiative public affairs director Erin Dick said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine that while it was encouraging the Airman in this situation knew enough to recognize the potential PCB exposure and say something, it is concerning to think of how many Airmen may have used such contaminated equipment over the decades before PCB hazards were fully known.

Dick said the Air Force should work to determine how widespread potential exposures were, identify and document anyone who may have been exposed, and make sure their health is monitored over the long term, potentially including screenings.

The Air Force said in its release that the Airman in this incident returned to duty “with no adverse effects.” But Dick said it could be too soon to make that conclusion.

“It’s really not possible to say, because of the way these chemicals work, if there will be long-term health effects for this particular Airman,” Dick said. “There is often a very long latency period before illnesses appear. But at least now he’s got [PCB exposure] documented, and that is something we’re trying to encourage all people who are currently serving [and those who previously served] in the community to make sure that their service is documented.”

Retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, a former commander of the 341st Missile Wing at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont., told Air & Space Forces Magazine the recent discovery of PCBs underscores how important it is for the Air Force to remain vigilant against these kind of contaminants.

As part of the Missile Community Cancer Study, the Air Force in 2023 took air and swipe samples from all three of its active ICBM bases: Malmstrom, F.E. Warren, and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. The swipe tests involve gauze wetted with a solution run over surfaces and then analyzed for suspected contaminants. The tests showed a few samples with elevated PCB levels at Minot and Malmstrom , while F.E. Warren had trace amounts not in excess of the EPA’s acceptable limit.

“Typically the command has been actually pretty good, once [PCBs have] been found, about dealing with them,” Reeves, now a senior resident fellow for space studies at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, said. “It’s really old stuff from back when we really weren’t tracking major chemicals and other things that are not good for humans. So now it’s about how well the command can react when things like this are found.”

Reeves said that because ICBMs still use many components from the years before PCBs were banned, the chemicals may still be out there in facilities. It’s crucial for the Air Force to keep looking for PCBs, she said, and the service needs to keep track and follow up with Airmen who may have come down with unusual conditions.

Air Force Global Strike Command also needs to come up with a way to go through its legacy equipment systematically and test them for PCBs, to make sure more potentially harmful gear isn’t out there, she said.

“The bigger context is not, ‘we found an isolated thing’” contaminated with PCBs, Reeves said. “This may be building a bigger picture that we may not yet be fully witting of.”

The post Air Force Pulls ICBM Testing Device After Finding Likely Carcinogen appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

items.body:
Lt. Gen. Jason D. Voorheis has taken command of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, a sprawling organization with a $400 billion portfolio, establishing him as one of the service’s top acquisition officials.

Voorheis moves into the job having jumped the rank of major general. As a one star, he was program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management , or C3BM, the office overseeing the Air Force’s effort to create a massive “battle network.”

Voorheis assumed command of AFLCMC on Aug. 27 during a ceremony at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, according to a release .

In his new role, Voorheis will also serve as the PAE for combat readiness and integrating PAE for mission systems.

AFLCMC has more than 21,000 employees and manages acquisition, upgrades, and support for aircraft, engines, munitions, electronics, and cyber systems. In other words, it’s the nerve center of keeping the service’s critical hardware running.

“Just about every aircraft, weapon system, uniform, and piece of gear our Airmen take into harm’s way is acquired, fielded, modernized, and sustained by the expertise within AFLCMC. You are the engine of our nation’s defense,” Voorheis told the center’s personnel at the ceremony.

Voorheis takes the post following the retirement of Lt. Gen. Donna D. Shipton , who also previously worked as the Integrating Program Executive Officer for Mission Systems.

Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams took over Voorheis’ previous role as the head of the C3BM office on Aug. 28, according to a separate release. The Air Force established C3BM in 2022, and Maj. Gen. Luke C.G. Cropsey served as its first commander, followed by Vorheis, who took over in February. Cropsey now serves as the military deputy to the Air Force acquisition executive in the Pentagon.

In bidding farewell to the C3BM office, Voorheis said his six months in the job included some of the “most rewarding experiences throughout my career.”

“The mission ahead does not pause,” Voorheis added. “Never stop challenging legacy processes that slow down capability delivery.”

The main goal of the C3BM office is to create a DAF Battle Network, an integrated system of systems that links sensor, effector, and logistics systems. With about 50 programs of record, it is the DAF’s piece of the Pentagon’s massive Combined Joint All Domain Command and Control effort, which seeks to connect any sensor, shooter, and logistics node to a shared network across all of the services.

But the three-star’s experience isn’t limited to the DAF Battle Network; he previously served as the program executive officer for fighters and advanced aircraft, the materiel leader for the F-15 program office, and system program director for the B-21 bomber, according to his official biography .

AFLCMC stood up in 2012 as part of an effort to consolidate and streamline operations within Air Force Materiel Command. It is one of six centers under AFMC, trimmed from a previous dozen centers the service operated, to lower costs, improve readiness, increase aircraft production, and reduce parts shortages, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.

The other centers under AFMC are the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center, the Air Force Test Center, the Air Force Installation Management Center, and the Air Force Sustainment Center.

items.body:
Just over a year ago, in July 2025, the Air Force established a dedicated office on the Air Staff for communications/cyber functions, separate from the intelligence directorate it had long been attached to. The new Warfighter Communications and Cyber Systems directorate now focuses on secure communications, cyber operations, and information technology systems as they support the frontline Airman or Guardian.

The move, leaders said at the time, was a major shakeup necessary to support the service’s need for resilient, reliable communications and cyber operations, and the equipment and personnel associated with those capabilities.

In June, Brig. Gen. Jeffrey A. Phillips took over as Deputy Chief of Staff for Warfighter Communications and Cyber Systems from interim deputy chief Brig. Gen. Joy Kaczor, who filled the role following the retirement of Maj. Gen. Michele C. Edmondson .

Phillips, a prior-enlisted Airman, started his career as a computer programmer and serving six years wearing stripes before commissioning through Officer Training School at Maxwell Air Force Base, Ala., in 1999. He previously commanded the 67th Cyberspace Wing at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, and served as Director of Cyberspace and Warfighting Communications at the headquarters of Air Combat Command at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va.

The one-star now serves a community of about 30,000 enlisted, 3,000 officers, and nearly 100 newly minted warrant officers. He recently sat down with Air & Space Forces Magazine for an interview about where the office stands after a year in operation and his priorities moving forward for the position, the equipment, and the people involved in vital communications and cyber work for the Air Force.

Editor’s Note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: What is your office doing to modernize both the equipment and support the Airmen in communications and cyber jobs?

A: We have to stop getting stuck in five-year acquisition cycles that end up delivering a product that’s outdated by the time we put it on the battlefield, and so that’s my number one priority. And we’re doing that through a few different lines of effort. Theater deployable communications, or TDC, is really important. We learned in operations like Operation Epic Fury that when we’re out in the field at several locations, we need to be connected at all those locations. So, we need to get that equipment out to the people who need to be connected, and we need to have Airmen out there who know how to operate it or make it simple enough for anyone to operate.

And there’s enterprise communications; those are the foundational networks that we connect back into from the edge, and a lot of those have been underinvested in over the past 30 years, so we’re playing a catch-up game. A big focus for Chief Information Officer Ashley Devoto and me is making sure we can modernize that enterprise network, so I came in with that as my number one priority.

My second priority is the continued evolution of our talent management processes. I think we’ve come a long way in the time that I’ve been part of it, and we need to do that for our enlisted Airmen, our warrant officers, and our officers. In the last few years, we created an executive development forum that all the cyber general officers sit on. It’s really a development team for our colonels. Now all of our general officers mentor all of our colonels.

This year we had what we call our Champions Initiative, and the colonels who were part of our development team were mentors to each O5 and below that we’re meeting on that development team. On the enlisted side, our 1D7 [Cyber Defense Operations] career field has obviously been in a state of flux and change for probably the last 10-plus years, we’ve changed those AFSCs and what they represented several times over that time period, and I kind of put a chalk line in the sand and I said we’re not going to make any more changes until we figure out what’s right, what’s wrong. We get the Airmen the career development courses that they need and then get them the education they need so they can test for promotions on their specialty knowledge tests. So that’s the number two priority.

There are a lot of key partners and stakeholders that we need to work with, so my goal is to rebuild those bridges because we can’t do anything alone. We have to partner with organizations like the Secretariat of the Air Force, the Office of the CIO, and DAF CIO Devoto. We have to partner with our acquisition organization, primarily under Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, and we work with the [Command, Control, Intelligence and Networks Directorate] within AFLCMC primarily for our theater deployable communication and our enterprise IT.

Q: What are some of the key technologies or equipment that your office is helping roll out, use, or upgrade across the communications and cyber areas of the Air Force?

A: Our legacy communication equipment is our Flexible Communication Package, or FCP. It’s been around probably for about the last decade. When you deploy an FCP, the only way a combatant commander can task it is through a unit type code that requires 10 pallet positions on an aircraft, about 40 people, and about 20 short tons to move. It includes things like bulldozers and huge satellite dishes, and it’s been modernized to the point that we don’t need such a big footprint anymore. Our new deployable comm kits—we have two of them: the ACP, the Agile Communications Package, and the Fly-Away Communications Terminal. They’re similar equipment, but a Fly-Away Comm Terminal supports fewer users than an ACP would. So, if we deploy somewhere we need to run command and control applications, we might need more compute and storage power. We can put that on the ACP. If we go someplace where we don’t have terrestrial internet, we can attach a satellite, our commercial satellite comm terminal. So agnostic transport is really big. We can set up a 5G bubble and use that as our transport. That gives us modular equipment so we can reduce our footprint and deploy with a couple of Airmen who know how to use it, providing connectivity for a whole mission-generation force element versus 10 pallet positions and, you know, 20 short tons.

We are in the midst of fielding ACPs. We have a lot of FACTs that are fielded. Now we’re working toward our next-generation ACPs. This technology changes very rapidly, and so keeping up with it is very challenging.

Q: You mentioned work to develop officers; what is your office trying to do for the enlisted and new warrant officers in the ranks?

The 1D7 Cyber Defense Operations career field, for example, has five “shreds.” At different points in time, there have been more or fewer shreds. Those shreds have meant different things, and so you could ask an Airman, or you could ask some senior leaders, “Hey, you know, what’s the definition of a 1D7X1 today? And unless you’re keeping up with the change, which was constant, it was very hard to define it clearly. So, freezing any further changes for Airmen in that career field is crucial because they want that stability, so they can develop more technical expertise and depth.

With warrant officers, we’re not asking them to lead people, we’re asking them to lead efforts. We’re asking them to become technical experts. We’ve put warrant officers in our cyberspace operations career field at the 67th Cyberspace Wing, and we’re starting to put them in the 688th [Cyberspace Wing] and get them into some staff positions as advisors to senior leaders who might not have the technical depth warrant officers have.

Q: How has working in Air Forces Cyber, and the cyber officer’s role, changed over the course of your time in uniform?

A: When I came in, we were support officers. Now we’re operations officers, and I think that’s a huge difference. I was proud of being a support officer. I had a great boss when I was a second lieutenant who pulled me in at Shaw Air Force Base, and he said, “Hey, Munster, this is your role as a communications officer at this base. You’re supporting the SEAD mission.” I said, “Sir. What’s the SEAD mission? He explained it as Suppression of Enemy Air Defenses, and I started to link my service to that mission, and I was very proud of that. As we transitioned to a more of an operational community, I got to lead a cyberspace operations squadron, and I saw how we were out there creating effects that supported whatever the goals of the operation might be, and I’m proud of that too. I think, you know, we’re proving that we are integral to most operations that happen.

The post Q&A: The Future of Air Force Cyber Systems and Warfighter Comms appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

items.body:
Inflation and rising costs for critical upgrades are swelling the price of the F-35 fighter, according to a newly released acquisition report on the fifth-generation jet .

The total estimated acquisition cost for the F-35—covering all the airframes and engines the U.S. government plans to buy—is now $536.2 billion, according to the latest modernized selected acquisition report the Pentagon released this month. That is $51 billion more than the $485.2 billion price tag recorded in the previous 2023 report, which represents more than 10 percent growth.

Other metrics included in the acquisition report show similar cost growth, such as the unit recurring flyaway cost—essentially the cost to produce one jet and its engine :

For the Air Force’s F-35A , the new flyaway cost is $78 million apiece in 2012 dollars, up 7.3 percent from the $72.7 million recorded in the last report.

For the F-35C carrier variant, flown by the Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, the new flyaway cost is $93.4 million in 2012 dollars, up 6.6 percent from the $87.65 million in the 2023 report

For the Marine Corps’ F-35B short takeoff and vertical landing variant, the most complex version, the flyaway cost is now $110.3 million in 2012 dollars, up 10.5 percent from $99.78 million.

The F-35 Joint Program Office, in response to queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine, declined to share the cost per variant for the latest F-35 lots in current-year dollars, saying that information is considered CUI, or controlled unclassified information, and is not releasable.

Nevertheless, the JPO did acknowledge the rise in costs and detailed some of the causes.

Research, development, test, and evaluation costs—which make up part of the overall total acquisition costs—have risen about $19 billion to $106.6 billion. The JPO said that growth reflects a refined estimate of the F-35’s Power Thermal Management Upgrade program to account for updated requirements and assumptions.

The F-35 program has also refined the schedule for the jet’s Block 4 modernization—a sweeping slate of upgrades intended to boost the F-35’s weapons, sensors, sensor fusion, and other capabilities—and engine core upgrade and power thermal management modernization efforts, which has added years and costs to the program, the JPO said.

The refinement of capability estimates for Block 4 accounted for about $900 million of that $19 billion growth in RDT&E costs, the JPO said.

The acquisition report said the F-35 program is prioritizing the delivery of 55 critical Block 4 capabilities, including kill chain enhancements for the F-35’s air superiority and suppression of enemy air defenses missions, and the integration of vital new weapons.

The JPO attributed another nearly $32 billion in procurement cost growth to incorporating the production costs of the F-35’s upcoming APG-85 radar, growth in production support costs, addition of the power thermal management upgrade production requirement, and incorporation of contractors’ actual costs, and the negotiated contract price of the F-35’s Lots 18 and 19 .

In September 2025, the Pentagon announced the F-35 JPO and Lockheed Martin had struck a final deal for Lots 18 and 19, to buy 296 aircraft for $24.29 billion. In April, the JPO and Pratt & Whitney announced deals worth a combined $6.6 billion for engines for Lots 18 and 19. Taken together, that points to an average cost across all variants of $104.4 million or so.

The report also pointed to rising inflation and material costs as other factors placing upward pressure on the F-35’s price tags.

The military plans to push some F-35 purchases into future “out-years” beyond the current budget cycle, the JPO said. The Marine Corps is also planning to shift some of its purchases away from F-35Bs and toward the carrier-based F-35Cs, the JPO said. Because the Marines will be buying F-35Cs further in the future than it had planned to buy F-35Bs, those carrier-based jets will be more expensive due to inflation and rising maintenance costs, further contributing to the program’s rising costs.

In the MSAR’s executive summary, the Pentagon called the F-35 program a “mature enterprise” with more than 1,200 jets operating in 20 nations, which is now focusing on long-term strategies for enhancing capabilities and bringing sustainment costs down. The report also pointed to progress made by the program, including the program entering into full-rate production in March 2024, and fielding aircraft with enhanced Technology Refresh 3 hardware that will pave the way for Block 4.

“The growing global demand speaks for itself,” the Pentagon said in the report. “The F-35’s value proposition is unmatched.”

Lockheed Martin, the primary manufacturer of the F-35, said in a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new report reflects a shift in the program’s focus toward modernizing the jet to take full advantage of its capabilities.

“The latest MSAR report shows the combat-proven F-35 program moving into full-rate production, resuming high-volume development deliveries and growing globally,” Mireya Villarreal, Lockheed’s spokesperson on the F-35 program, said in an email. “It also shows that the hard work has shifted from proving the basic aircraft to executing major modernizaiton, improving fleet readiness, and controlling long-term sustainment and integration costs.”

The post F-35 Price Rising due to New Upgrades, Inflation, More appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

items.title: Guidance: Ex-Gratia Medical Payments reviews
items.summary: Guidance for former locally employed staff who were injured in the course of their service.
items.body:
Overview

The UK government initiated the Ex-Gratia Medical Payments (EGMP) policy to provide support to former locally-employed staff in Afghanistan who were injured as a result of their employment with the Ministry of Defence ( MOD ) between 2001 and 2021. The EGMP scheme was closed to new applications in 2021.

The EGMP Review was initiated in June 2020 to enable reviews of payments under the EGMP.

As of 23 July 2026, the EGMP review is closed to new applications. Those who have already applied will also no longer be able to provide further evidence on their applications.

All applications received before the scheme closed will be processed.

No new applications are being accepted.

This publication explains the eligibility criteria for the EGMP Review.

Background

Between 2001 and 2021, local staff in Afghanistan who worked with the UK government played an important part in our joint efforts towards the shared goal of a more secure, stable and prosperous Afghanistan.

Extremely brave people worked alongside our soldiers on patrol, and in some cases suffered profoundly life-changing injuries as a result of enemy action. The government committed to awarding appropriate payments for these people through the EGMP.

In 2020, the MOD initiated a process for reviewing the EGMP cases relating to individuals who wish to have their cases re-assessed. Its intent was to enable those whose condition has deteriorated beyond their original prognosis, or those who have developed a late-onset condition, to receive a fair full and final payment without prejudice.

Eligibility Criteria

To be eligible for the EGMP Review, the applicant must satisfy all of the following criteria:

The injury must have occurred during MOD employment and have been recorded by the Department at the time;

AND

2. There must be sufficient evidence that the condition has deteriorated beyond what was assessed as the projected recovery at the time, or that a new condition has arisen as a result of the original injury;

For EGMP Review applications received prior to 23 April 2026, these must have been reported to us within 3 years of formal diagnosis of the deterioration or new condition (as opposed to 3 years of the date of initial award payment for applications submitted on or after 23 April 2026). Consideration will also be given to cases where eligibility to the EGMP was previously considered but a payment was not awarded, where evidence supports this;

For EGMP Review applications received prior to 23 April 2026, these must have been reported to us within 3 years of formal diagnosis of the deterioration or new condition (as opposed to 3 years of the date of initial award payment for applications submitted on or after 23 April 2026). Consideration will also be given to cases where eligibility to the EGMP was previously considered but a payment was not awarded, where evidence supports this;

For EGMP Review applications received after 23 April 2026 these must have been reported to us within 3 years of the initial EGMP award unless the condition could clearly not have been known to the individual within that timescale;

For EGMP Review applications received after 23 April 2026 these must have been reported to us within 3 years of the initial EGMP award unless the condition could clearly not have been known to the individual within that timescale;

AND

3. The deterioration or new condition must be a significant permanent physical or mental impairment or disability, including any serious scarring or disfigurement.

These payments are not intended to provide compensation for those injuries where the individual is expected to make a complete recovery or where they may be left with some permanent or long-lasting impairment of a less serious nature, for example limited in either the degree of pain or loss of faculty.

Making a claim

New claims are no longer being accepted as of the 23 July 2026. All applications received before the scheme closed will be processed.

Prior to the closure of the scheme, claims were required to be submitted before 23 July 2026 using the Ex-Gratia Medical Review Claim Form to DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk , together with photocopies of two forms of identification: either a passport or a driving license, and a utility bill showing the claimant’s current address dated within the previous three months.

The panel’s decision will be communicated in writing.

Receiving your payment

A decision on your application to the EGMP Review will be communicated to you electronically from DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk .

If a Review payment is awarded to you, this will be on a full and final settlement basis without prejudice. You will be asked to sign your understanding of this before the payment can be made. You will also be asked to provide your bank details. Upon receipt of these, the payment will be made as soon as is practically possible.

Appealing the review decision

In the event you are not satisfied with the outcome of your application to the EGMP Review, you can appeal the decision within 12 months of being sent the outcome letter. You can appeal the review decision by contacting DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk and setting out why you are not satisfied with the outcome and why you consider this should be looked at again, with any relevant evidence to support your appeal.

items.title: NATO Submarine Rescue System conducts Exercise Flying Fish
items.summary: The NATO submarine rescue system tests global RAF airlift capability in major exercise, keeping UK, France and Norway crews emergency ready.
items.body:
The NATO Submarine Rescue System (NSRS) has taken part in an exercise to prove it can be flown, by the Royal Air Force, to anywhere in the world.

A tri-national government capability jointly owned by France, Norway and the UK, the NSRS is one of the world’s leading submarine rescue capabilities.

Developed to be fully air-mobile, this global capability can evacuate stricken submariners from a submarine disabled on the seabed at depths down to 610 metres.

With 350 tonnes of unique equipment that needs 27 lorries and several aircraft to mobilise, this exercise was key to proving the system can respond quickly.

An important part of the rapid response needed for a submarine emergency is transporting the system by road to an airport, which on this occasion was RAF Brize Norton.

A police escort was practised during the event, with every police force between Glasgow and Brize Norton used to provide a constant blue light presence to the convoy.

Once at Brize Norton, the Submarine Rescue Vehicle, effectively a mini-submarine, was loaded on a simulator with the exact dimensions and deck arrangement of a C-17A Globemaster. Some of the heaviest support equipment was also loaded onto a similar simulator for the A400M Atlas military transport aircraft.

This was the first use of the A400M Atlas for NSRS transport and means the aircraft can now be used by UK and NATO partner nations’ air forces for future mobilisation, enhancing the ability for rapid deployment of NSRS. Both loading events were conducted by the specialist RAF team at the Joint Air Delivery Test and Evaluation Unit.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:

This is a piece of specialist equipment we hope never to have to use, but the ability to mobilise the NATO Submarine Rescue System at short notice to anywhere in the world is reassuring for the UK and our allies.

If a submarine is in trouble we will need to respond fast. Ensuring we have a tried and tested response is how we can be ready for any eventuality.

Captain Lyons RN, Operating Duty Holder for the NSRS, who witnessed the operation, said:

Rescue of the crew from a stricken submarine will require numerous agencies to operate efficiently as one team, and this loading exercise on to a military aircraft is a vital aspect to maintain training and currency for our RAF colleagues.

I was delighted to see them maintain efficient and close control of this unique vehicle that is relied upon by so many nations.

The exercise tempo for all parts of the system is relentless, as it must provide assurance to all our partner nations that the NSRS remains rescue ready.

The NSRS is delivered on behalf of the Royal Navy, Marine Nationale, and Norwegian Navy by the DNE’s Submarine Delivery Group, with JFD Global as the service contractor.

items.summary: Information on childcare for Service families within the UK and overseas.
items.body:
Wraparound Childcare

Known as ‘Out of School Care’ in Wales and ‘School age childcare’ in Scotland.

Childcare is a concern that continues to be raised on behalf of Service families by the Families Federations and other stakeholders. The concern has been reflected in recent surveys carried out by the Families Federations, the wider Armed Forces Continuous Attitude Survey ( AFCAS ) and the Families Continuous Attitude Survey ( FAMCAS ).

Feedback from AFCAS and FAMCAS highlighted that a lack of good-quality, enriching and appropriate childcare has a significant impact on partner employment, which can influence Service personnels’ decisions on whether to stay in or leave the Armed Forces.

In recognition of the issues that some Service families face when trying to access wraparound childcare and its potential negative impact on retention, Defence launched the Wraparound Childcare ( WAC ) Scheme in September 2022.

Eligible Service personnel (Tri-Service) can register for up to 20 hours a week per child during term time only (39 weeks per year) of wraparound childcare funding for 4 to 11-year-old children (4 to 16 years if in receipt of certain disability benefits) attending before and after school childcare in the UK or eligible overseas locations.

WAC funding does not provide childcare spaces, it is funding for costs incurred when eligible families pay for before and after school childcare.

Eligibility criteria for WAC

The scheme is open to regular and full-time reserve service (FTRS) (all commitment types) personnel. Service personnel will be eligible following their completion of Phase 1 training until their termination date.

The Service person must either be assigned within the UK, overseas within the European Economic Area and Switzerland (EEA&S), overseas using a Defence Children Services (DCS) childcare provider, or unaccompanied in other overseas locations with their family remaining in the UK, the EEA&S or an overseas location using a DCS provider for before and after school childcare.

The child for whom the Service person has parental responsibility must be aged 4 to 11 years (4 to 16 years if in receipt of certain UK disability benefits), must attend school (including home education) and be living with the serving person for at least 50% of the time unless separated due to Service commitments (deployment, residential courses), or when serving on unaccompanied assignments overseas with the family remaining in the UK, EEA&S or overseas location and using a DCS provider for before and after school childcare.

An active Tax-Free Childcare ( TFC ) account must be set up with HRMC for each child that a Service person wants to claim funding for. Active means that you reconfirm your account every 3 months and receive the 20% top-up from HMRC when you add money into the account and when using UK or DCS childcare providers, or receive the 20% top-up from the manual TFC process if using host nation childcare providers within the EEA&S.

The childcare provider must either be: located in the UK and be OFSTED-registered (or equivalent) and accept TFC payments; a DCS childcare setting (if spaces are available) which accepts TFC payments; or located overseas in the EEA&S and is registered, regulated and inspected by host nation authorities.

The Service person and their partner (or a sole parent in a single parent family) must be in paid employment, self-employed, starting or re-starting work within the next 31 days, and have a weekly income equivalent to at least 16 hours at the UK National Minimum or Living Wage .

Both parents (or a sole parent in a single parent family) must each have an adjusted net income of £100,000 or less per annum.

Primary School Aged Childcare Overseas (PSACO) Allowance

The final phase of the Defence Wraparound Childcare ( WAC ) scheme roll-out. The PSACO Allowance provides a reimbursement of costs for before and after school childcare in overseas locations where due to local rules or regulations it is not possible for WAC eligibility criteria to be met, or because Tax-Free Childcare ( TFC ) accounts are not available.

The PSACO Allowance does not provide childcare spaces, it provides funding for costs incurred when eligible families pay for before and after school childcare.

Eligibility criteria for the PSACO Allowance

The scheme is open to regular and full-time reserve service (FTRS) (all commitment types) personnel. Service personnel will be eligible following their completion of Phase 1 training until their termination date.

The child for whom the Service person has parental responsibility must be: aged 4 to 11 years (4 to 16 years if in receipt of certain UK disability benefits) must attend school (including home education) full time be living with the serving person for at least 50% of the time unless separated due to Service commitments.

United Kingdom (UK)

There are a number of childcare options for parents to choose from. Parents should go to the Best Start in Life website for further information and guidance on all available government childcare schemes.

Check to see if you’re eligible for Tax-Free Childcare ( TFC ) . You can get TFC at the same time as Government funded childcare hours if you’re eligible for both.

England

Working families are entitled to 30 hours per week for 38 weeks of the year for children aged 9 months to school starting age.​ All families are entitled to 15 hours per week for 38 weeks of the year for children aged from 3-years-old to school starting age.

For further information, please visit the Best Start in Life website .

You can also check to see if you’re eligible for Tax-Free Childcare ( TFC ). You can get TFC at the same time as 15 or 30 hours’ free childcare if you’re eligible for both.

Scotland

Funded early learning and childcare is free to all parents and is funded by the Scottish Government. You can get up to 1,140 hours of funded early learning and childcare per year (around 30 hours a week in term time) if your child is 3 or 4 years old. Some 2-year-old children are also eligible.

For more information, please visit Help paying for childcare .

Wales

Wales provides a minimum of 10 hours per week of nursery education for all children aged 3 to 4 years; up to an additional 20 hours per week of funded childcare for eligible parents of 3 to 4-year-old children during term-time, rising to 30 hours of funded childcare for up to 9 weeks during school holidays.

For further information about the childcare offer in Wales, parents should visit the Welsh Government website .

Northern Ireland

Parents of children aged 3 and 4 years old can apply to receive 12.5 hours a week of free, also known as ‘funded’ pre-school education. This allocation can only be taken over 2.5 hours per day, 5 days a week during term time.

Places are provided by nursery schools, primary schools with nursery units and some voluntary and private providers. The places cannot be provided by childminders.

For more information, please visit NI Direct .

For further information and guidance about the childcare offer in Northern Ireland, parents should contact 38 (Irish) Brigade at RC-AWS-N-38X-0mailbox@mod.gov.uk .

Defence UK Nursery Authority (UKNA)

The UKNA is a Defence scheme that will reimburse eligible working parents in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland for the difference in the costs of Early Years childcare hours, matching the “free” (Government funded) childcare hours they would be entitled to if assigned to England.

UKNA does not provide childcare spaces.

In England, working families can access 30 hours of Government funded childcare per child for 38 weeks annually. Through the UKNA scheme, from September 2026, eligible Armed Forces families may register to claim back the costs for the difference between English and Devolved Government funded hours.

Subject to ongoing eligibility, UKNA funding stops when the child start full-time education (P1 or home education).

Subject to ongoing eligibility, UKNA funding stops when the child start full-time education (P1 or home education).

Service personnel should read the UKNA DIN for information about when eligibility ceases. Search UK Nursery Authority at DINs Search (defnet) or Group: Defence Instruction Notices - DIN’s | Defence Connect . (Service personnel only).

If you already receive free early years childcare hours from the Government in your location (Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland), Defence will reimburse you for the cost of extra hours to make the maximum number of funded hours that you will receive up to 30 hours per week. E.g. if you receive 12.5 hours per week for your child, Defence will reimburse you for the cost of 17.5 hours per week for 38 weeks per year.

Eligibility criteria for UKNA

Eligibility criteria for working parents of children aged between 9 months and 3 years old in Scotland and Wales, and 9 months to 4 years old in Northern Ireland, from September 2026.

Regular or Full Time Reserve Service (Full Commitment) personnel.

How to register and claim

Registration and claims information is available on the UKNA section of Discover My Benefits .

Contact

For queries about claims please contact your unit HR team or admin office.

For policy questions, email: PEOPLE-AFFS-CHILD-EXPENSES@Mod.gov.uk .

For more information on UKNA visit: Defence childcare information (accessible by MOD personnel only) or Defence Connect (sign-in required).

Moving to England from overseas or within the UK

If you are returning from overseas or moving within the UK, please visit the Best Start in Life website to find out what is available in your area. The application process and deadlines may vary.

It’s not possible to apply for additional funded childcare online when you are outside England. If you are due to return to England from overseas or elsewhere in the UK after a term deadline, you can call the Childcare Service Helpline on 0300 123 4097 to apply for a free childcare code and request a manual application. The manual application must be completed before the term deadline.

Information on term deadlines and when to apply can be found in DIN - Early years funded childcare overseas. Search for the DIN on defnet or Defence Connect (accessible by MOD personnel only).

Parents can apply outside of the recommended dates, but they might not receive their code in time. Parents must have a valid code by the end of the month before a new term starts.

Overseas

In overseas locations, the Ministry of Defence ( MOD ) provides services (or access to services) that, so far as is reasonably practicable, conform in type, scope and standard to that required by legislation in England.

items.body:
WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio -- In a show of artificial intelligence in space, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) recently demonstrated autonomous control of a satellite bus using a neural network. The flight marks a pivotal shift from AI managing sensors and payloads to it directly commanding the critical function of spacecraft orientation.

During the mission, an AI agent was uplinked to a CubeSat orbiting hundreds of miles above Earth. Within a single orbit and without human intervention, the neural network autonomously controlled the spacecraft's orientation, precisely steering the vehicle to its mission objective and avoiding hazardous conditions

"We have a responsibility to translate advances in AI to give our Airmen and Guardians trustworthy autonomous teammates to meet today's fast-moving challenges,” said Department of the Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL Commander Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert . “The AFRL vision is to win the future by executing our mission to discover, develop and deliver war-winning science and technology."

~ Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert, Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL Commander

AFRL's Autonomy Capability Team (ACT3) trained the neural network using reinforcement learning and subjected it to extensive pre-flight simulation and laboratory testing, bridging the gap between simulated environments and physical operations ahead of uploading it to the test vehicle.

“We used startup-like agility to take a reinforcement learning model from the lab directly to orbit,” said Dr. Steve “Cap” Rogers , AFRL senior scientist for AI enabled autonomy. “This flight is a perfect example of ACT3's core mission to operationalize AI at scale for the Air and Space Force.”

To ensure mission safety, the flight also tested a next-generation AI watchdog system and AFRL-designed guardrail runtime assurance systems. Watchdogs detect when AI systems approach unverified situations, enabling them to pivot seamlessly to backup systems. Guardrails monitor vehicle state and neural network outputs, intervening when predefined safety boundaries are approached. These systems ran in “shadow mode” and provided insight to how each would respond to the neural network in real time.

With the foundational capabilities of neural network control now proven in orbit, AFRL plans to expand the scope and complexity of autonomous operations for future flights.

About AFRL The Air Force Research Laboratory is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and the multidomain. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit: afresearchlab.com .

About ACT3 AFRL’s ACT3 is an AI Special Operations organization whose mission is to Operationalize AI at Scale for the Air Force and the Space Force. Commissioned by the AFRL Commander, ACT3 leverages an innovative ‘start-up’ business model as an alternative approach to the traditional AFRL Technical Directorate R&D model by combining the blue sky vision of an academic institution; the flexibility of an AI startup; and the discipline of a production development company. The goal of the ACT3 business model is to define the shortest path to successful transition of solutions using AFRL’s internal expertise and collaborations with the best academic and commercial AI researchers in the world. Successful implementation may mean new technology or new implementation of existing technology. To learn more about ACT3, visit: afrl.af.mil/ACT3/

items.summary: This week's photos feature Airmen from around the globe involved in activities supporting expeditionary operations and defending America. This weekly feature showcases the men and women of the Air Force.

items.title: Master your mind: AFGSC reimagines readiness with MindGym
items.author: Tech. Sgt. Shelby Thurman
items.summary: To ensure operational readiness & maintain the tactical edge, Airmen must train their brains with the same rigor as their bodies. AFGSC is looking to accelerate & modernize this effort with a tactical training simulator known as MindGym.

items.title: 'Final denial': Air Force leaders lean into future of drone defense
items.author: 2nd Lt. Daniel White
items.summary: The 31st Air Task Force sharpened and refined a layered counter-small unmanned aerial system defense capability, culminating in a kinetic “final denial” live-fire demonstration.

items.title: Operation TREK808: PACAF, HING rapidly provide critical aid to Hawaii Island recovery
items.author: Maj. Nicolle Roose
items.summary: PACAF and the Hawaii National Guard partnered with federal and state agencies to execute Operation TREK808, airlifting nearly 144,000 pounds of critical utility infrastructure and repair vehicles to Hawaii Island.

items.title: Spin it to win it: McConnell AFB innovation
items.author: Airman Daniel Obi
items.summary: A 3D-printed tool designed by a McConnell AFB maintainer is helping Airmen refinish aircraft wheels faster by allowing them to rotate the wheels while painting, eliminating hours of drying time between coats.

items.title: Tyndall AFB sharpens air-to-ground capabilities during Combat Hammer
items.author: Senior Airman Amanda Alvarez
items.summary: The 325th FW deployed to Hill AFB to test and evaluate the F-35A Lightning II's air-to-ground precision-guided munitions capability using live ordnance.

items.title: Eglin AFB Airmen mobilize for life-saving medical flight
items.author: Samuel King Jr.
items.summary: When the 413th Flight Test Squadron receives a call from the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center, it's typically the last resort for someone in the community requiring a life-saving critical care flight.

items.title: Readout of USAF Chief of Staff Gen. Wilsbach’s counterpart visit with Bulgarian AF Commander Maj. Gen. Nikolay Rusev
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: Bilateral talks at the Pentagon focused on NATO burden-sharing, eastern flank collective deterrence and Bulgaria’s acquisition of eight F-16 Block 70 fighter aircraft.

items.title: Hernandez-Baquero swears in as Department of the Air Force space acquisition and integration lead
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: Dr. Erich "HB" Hernandez-Baquero was sworn in as the second Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Space Acquisition and Integration during a Pentagon ceremony this morning, following his confirmation to the role by the U.S. Senate, Aug. 7.

items.title: Air Force awards production contract for next-gen Aerospace Readiness Enterprise System
items.author: Dan Hawkins
items.summary: The DAF’s initiative to overhaul its aircrew management systems has reached a critical milestone following extensive operator testing, officially awarding the ARES production contract to VivSoft.
